item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.5.0: Full ONVIF Protocol Support + Hardware Transcoding + rpi-cam Co-development
item.description:
Less than a week after v0.4.0, v0.5.0 is a feature-dense release: full ONVIF protocol support (covering all five major services: Device/Media/PTZ/Imaging/Event), hardware transcoding (H.265 → H.264), and recorder reconnection optimizations. See the full changelog at GitHub Release Notes.

If you haven’t seen the previous versions, check out MiBeeNvr Introduction and v0.4.0 Technical Post.

Full ONVIF Protocol Support

v0.4.0 already had ONVIF device discovery and stream URL retrieval, but that was just the tip of the ONVIF iceberg. v0.5.0 completes the core services of ONVIF Profile S:

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.6.0: Timelapse + Transcoding UI + ONVIF Enhancements + Documentation Restructure
item.description: Once recording is up and running, storage becomes the first bottleneck. A single 1080p camera writes tens of GB per day — with a 30-day retention policy, a 1TB drive is mostly consumed. Many community members reported the same issue, and during discussions, the ideas of timelapse and transcoding storage gained the most traction: most of the time the scene is static, and compressing it with timelapse requires only 5% of the space for the same duration.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.9.0 → v0.9.1: ONVIF Zero-Config Auto-Discovery + Storage Rewrite + Lock-Free Camera Manager + Optional FFmpeg + Full i18n Repair
item.description: Nine cameras were hanging off a Banana Pi M5, and a few pieces of engineering debt had reached the point where they needed paying off. The /api/cameras endpoint would stall for 14.9 seconds while all 9 recorders started up — not because the traversal was slow, but because the cm.mu RWMutex was blocking, holding every read operation out. ONVIF camera addition still required typing in IP addresses manually, and with a household of CW500s, DS-2CD2047G2s, and others, every new camera meant opening a terminal session — not sustainable. FFmpeg as the only third-party binary dependency meant every deployment needed a check for whether it was installed, and on Raspberry Pi you also had to worry about hardware encoder compatibility. And the older Xiaomi devices — Dafang, Xiaofang, Aqara G2 — couldn’t be integrated at all because they speak the TUTK protocol. None of these are new technical challenges; they’re engineering debt, and v0.9 pays it off in one shot.

item.title: ONVIF vs GB/T 28181: How They Work Inside — Plug-and-Play Devices vs System-Level Networking
item.description: After MiBeeNvr v0.9 shipped ONVIF auto-discovery, manual camera configuration was mostly gone. The next question was whether to add GB/T 28181 uplink support, so I dug through the mechanics of both protocols. Most comparison articles online stop at “ONVIF is the international standard, GB28181 is the Chinese national standard”—which carries zero information for someone writing code. This post breaks both protocols down to the signaling-flow and message level: how ONVIF discovers devices and obtains stream URIs; how GB28181’s 20-digit codes address everything, how INVITE negotiates a stream, and what PS encapsulation actually is.

item.title: PTZ Latency End-to-End: From Encoding to Transport Optimization
item.description:
The operator calls: the PTZ feed is several seconds behind. Push the joystick and the far end reacts long after. Ops swaps the camera first—no change; suspects the network—RTT measured, normal; finally shrinks the player buffer—the problem disappears on the spot.

That is not a skit; it is the standard path of a “latency complaint”: swap hardware first, check the network second, and only then get to the real problem. The previous post in this series, “The Two Devils of PTZ Cameras,” named latency one of the two devils. This one tears it apart: where each millisecond goes, what can be optimized, and what is a hard protocol limitation.

item.title: The Surveillance Protocol Panorama: A Four-Layer Map from Access to Compliance — What Each Protocol Is and When to Use It
item.description: The previous post took ONVIF and GB/T 28181 apart down to signaling and messages. But building an NVR means the protocol environment extends well beyond those two: vendor-private APIs on the camera side, a view-library standard on the public-security side, Ministry-of-Transport standards for vehicles, WebRTC for browser viewing, HLS for public distribution, and a national-crypto compliance stack. This post lays out the entire landscape—each protocol gets four sections: what it is → key technical points → its relationship with other protocols → its value to an NVR. Beginners can read it as an index; veterans can jump straight to the priority table.

item.title: Dual-Stack Cameras in the Field: What Happens When ONVIF and GB28181 Run Together, and Whether GB28181 Travels
item.description:
The first two posts covered protocol mechanics and the landscape; this one returns to device-side questions an NVR builder actually meets: can a camera hang both protocol stacks at once? With both enabled, what does it cost the camera, and what does it mean for an NVR that discovers cameras via ONVIF? Finally, a product question—does GB28181 actually get used overseas, and is it worth building for international markets?

item.title: The Rust and Go Ecosystems for ONVIF/GB28181: Library Selection, Source Reading, and a Hardware-Free Integration Path
item.description: The first three posts settled the protocol mechanics, the landscape, and the device side; the final question is concrete: which libraries to write it with. This survey went through everything usable in both ecosystems. The one-sentence verdict: ONVIF has workable libraries on both sides; the mature GB28181 implementations live on the Go/Java/C++ side while Rust’s are still young; and for streaming infrastructure (repackaging, distribution, egress) the Go ecosystem is clearly thicker.

item.title: Taking Over onvif-go: Real-Camera Fixes, Zero Dependencies, and Service Facades
item.description:
MiBeeNvr talks to cameras over ONVIF, and this library is what sits underneath. ONVIF is the de facto standard for IP video surveillance equipment: device discovery, media profiles, PTZ control, event subscriptions — all one set of SOAP-over-HTTP service conventions. Any brand that claims ONVIF compliance can, in theory, be integrated through the same calls.

onvif-go is that stack implemented in Go. We did not write it from scratch: its upstream was 0x524a/onvif-go — the previous author reshaped it into its modern form of a client plus a virtual camera server (the git history still traces back to earlier Go ONVIF attempts in the community). But upstream stalled entering 2026: the last merged PR landed in mid-January, the v1.0-through-v1.1.3 release cadence from late 2025 never resumed, and three Improve Test Coverage issues filed in November 2025 sit unclaimed to this day. Meanwhile we hit two problems in our own camera pool that could only be fixed inside the library.
